newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China army unit makes low-key entry into Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: China army unit makes low-key entry into Hong Kong.

text.p: An advance guard of China's army rolled quietly into Hong Kong on Monday, preparing the ground for the territory's return to Chinese rule after 150 years of British rule.

The arrival of the small unarmed unit of the People's Liberation Army (PLA), with 71 days to go before Britain hands over its last important colony, was low-key and left many of the wealthy territory's six million people unmoved.

But as the convoy carrying 40 Chinese soldiers navigated crowded city streets, some democracy advocates, who recall the Chinese military's role in suppressing dissent in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989, questioned their presence.
There was no pomp and little ceremony when the PLA party led by Major-General Zhou Borong drove across the border to Hong Kong.
Zhou emerged from his black Audi staff car to be greeted by a Chinese diplomat stationed in Hong Kong but his soldiers remained inside their vehicles, staring ahead impassively.

They arrived as Hong Kong argued about civil liberties after the handover, but the advance party, whose task is to prepare facilities for the full garrison due on July 1, is expected to play no part in internal Hong Kong affairs.

As the clock ticks away to the end of a British era in Asia at midnight on June 30, Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp is squabbling with the territory's post-colonial leader who supports China's proposals to dilute civil liberties laws.

Martin Lee, leader of the largest pro-democracy party in Hong Kong, returned on Monday from the United States where he met President Bill Clinton and obtained considerable support for his campaign opposing the proposed changes.
Hong Kong's future leader, former shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa, recently cancelled his own plans to visit the United States to explain why he thinks the China-endorsed changes are needed.

He argues that replacing Hong Kong's elected legislature with one crafted by Beijing, and legislative changes to curb demonstrations and ban foreign funding for political groups, will not fundamentally damage freedoms in the bustling community.
The advance PLA party will live alongside the remaining British soldiers in the Prince of Wales barracks and at a naval base on nearby Stonecutters Island.
But few in Hong Kong expect to see the Chinese relaxing in Hong Kong's bars or nightclubs with British troops and American sailors from U.S. warships visiting the port.

"Many people in Hong Kong have mixed feelings about the PLA, a lot of which is in fact fear; so the behaviour of the PLA, the first contingent of the PLA in Hong Kong, will certainly have an impact on how Hong Kong will see the arrival of the Chinese government and its representatives," said Democratic Party member Huang Chen-ya.
But a middle-aged Hong Kong woman, among the sparse crowds who stood on overpasses for a glimpse of the new arrivals, said she was not concerned. "What is there to fear?" she asked.

Hong Kong's stock exchange, which long ago digested the coming fundamental changes in the territory, showed no qualms. The Hang Seng Index ended higher on the strength of companies involved in the sky-high property market.

British soldiers waiting at the border climbed in beside PLA drivers to guide the eight-vehicle convoy to the harbour-side Prince of Wales Barracks in the shadow of gleaming skyscrapers in the central business district.
For decades, British and Chinese soldiers have patrolled the border between Communist China and capitalist Hong Kong, passing on occasions just metres from each other.
Until recently their lives were a world apart.

The commander of the future PLA garrison in Hong Kong is no longer a stranger to the territory -- he has visited twice in the past year as a guest of the Commander of British Forces Major-General Bryan Dutton.
Rugby-playing members of the future PLA garrison, based just over the border in the southern city of Shenzhen, have taken on their British counterparts in tournaments in Hong Kong.
Dutton welcomed the PLA troops on the steps of the barracks.

"We intend to ensure that the garrison gives the PLA every possible assistance in their preparations," he said in remarks competing with the rumble of nearby construction sites and traffic noise which form a 24-hour backdrop to Hong Kong life.
"Huanying, huanying (welcome, welcome)," he added in Chinese.
Earlier, the British garrison celebrated Queen Elizabeth's birthday with a 21-gun salute from the Royal Navy patrol ship HMS Starling, anchored nearby in the harbour.

But there was no pipe and drum band welcome in Hong Kong from the resident British regiment, the Black Watch, for the PLA contingent, who had been given a rousing send-off from China, departing to the strains of the "March of the PLA".
"This is the first time the PLA have been on Hong Kong soil," a British spokeswoman said. "Our guiding principle is to be as helpful as possible."
"It's interesting," said Sergeant Paul Keenan of the arrival of the communist troops. "It's a thing to tell your kids about when you're older."
